lessons.title: Screen Printing on Glass
lessons.body: Screen printing is the most common way to decorate glass in small African workshops. You need a wooden or aluminium frame, a mesh screen (usually 110â160 threads per inch for glass), a squeegee, and UV-curable or air-dry glass paint. For a simple one-colour logo on 500 ml bottles, start by stretching the mesh tightly over the frame and securing it with staples or glue. Coat the screen with photo emulsion in a dark room, let it dry, then expose it to sunlight with your design printed on a transparent film for 2â5 minutes. Wash out the unexposed emulsion with a gentle spray of water. Now you have a stencil. Place the screen on a clean glass surface, apply a bead of paint across the top, and pull the squeegee firmly at a 60â70Â° angle. For glass, use a hard squeegee (70 durometer). Cure the print: if using UV paint, pass under a UV lamp for 30â60 seconds; if air-dry, let it sit for 24 hours. In Africa, many workshops use locally available screen printing supplies from Kenya, Nigeria, or South Africa. A common problem is paint bleeding under the stencilâfix it by adding more tension to the screen or using a thicker emulsion. For multi-colour prints, you need one screen per colour and must register them carefully. Start with single-colour jobs like branding on drinking glasses or window decals. Always wear gloves and work in a well-ventilated area. With practice, you can print 100â200 pieces per hour. Clean your screen immediately with the recommended solvent, or the paint will harden and ruin the mesh.

lessons.title: Digital Printing and Decals
lessons.body: Digital printing and decals let you put full-colour, detailed images on glass without making a screen. The two main methods are direct UV printing and water-slide decals. For direct printing, you need a UV flatbed printer (costly, but many African print shops rent time on them). You design your artwork in CorelDRAW or Photoshop, then print directly onto the glass with UV-curable ink. The printer cures the ink instantly with UV light. This works best on flat glass like windows, mirrors, or tiles. For curved or small items, use water-slide decals. You print your design on special decal paper using a normal inkjet or laser printer. Then you spray it with a clear lacquer to protect the ink. Soak the decal in water for 30â60 seconds, slide it onto the clean glass, and smooth out air bubbles with a soft squeegee. Let it dry for 24 hours, then bake in an oven at 150Â°C for 30 minutes to make it dishwasher-safe. In Africa, decals are popular for personalised gifts like mugs, bottles, and awards. You can buy decal paper from online suppliers or local ceramic shops. A key tip: clean the glass with alcohol before applying any decal, or it will peel. For small-scale production, a heat press can help adhere decals evenly. If you don't have a printer, you can order custom decals from print shops in cities like Nairobi, Lagos, or Johannesburg. Always test on a scrap piece first. Digital printing gives you photo-quality results, but it's slower and more expensive per piece than screen printing for simple designs. Use it for short runs, complex images, or personalised items.

lessons.title: Painting and Staining
lessons.body: Painting and staining glass by hand is a low-cost way to add colour and design. You need glass paints (solvent-based or water-based), fine brushes, masking tape, and a clean workspace. For staining, you can use glass stain that is transparent and lets light through, or opaque paint for solid colours. Start by cleaning the glass with methylated spirits to remove any grease. If you want sharp lines, apply masking tape to create borders or patterns. For a simple stained-glass effect, use lead-free outliner to draw the design, let it dry, then fill in with glass paint. Solvent-based paints dry in 24 hours and are more durable; water-based paints are easier to clean up but need a topcoat. In Africa, many artisans use locally made glass paints from South Africa or imported brands. A common technique is 'reverse painting' on the back of glassâyou paint the details first, then the background, so the front looks perfect. For bottles or vases, you can dip them in coloured glass stain or use a sponge for a textured look. Baking the painted glass at 160Â°C for 30 minutes makes it more resistant to washing. Always work in a dust-free area; dust ruins the finish. If you make a mistake, wipe it off immediately with a solvent before it dries. For large panels, work in sections. You can also mix paint with a medium to make it flow better. Practice on small pieces first. Hand-painted glass sells well for gifts, church windows, and decorative panels. With a steady hand and a few brushes, you can create unique pieces that stand out.

lessons.title: Lamination and Coloring
lessons.body: Lamination and coloring involve bonding coloured interlayers between two sheets of glass, usually under heat and pressure. This is common for safety glass, but also for decorative panels. The most basic method uses EVA (ethylene vinyl acetate) film, which you can buy in rolls. You cut the film to size, place it between two clean glass sheets, and put the sandwich in a vacuum bag. Then you heat it in an oven or kiln at 120â140Â°C for 30â60 minutes. The vacuum removes air bubbles, and the EVA melts and bonds the glass. After cooling, you have a coloured, laminated glass panel. For more vibrant colours, use coloured PVB (polyvinyl butyral) interlayers, which come in many shades. These require higher pressure (10â12 bar) and temperature (140â150Â°C) in an autoclaveâexpensive equipment, so many small workshops outsource this step. In Africa, EVA lamination is popular because it's affordable and can be done with a simple vacuum bag and a kitchen oven. You can also add fabrics, leaves, or paper between the glass layers for a unique look. Always work in a clean room; any dust becomes a permanent bubble. Cut the film 2â3 mm smaller than the glass to avoid overflow. After lamination, trim excess film with a sharp blade. For coloring without lamination, you can use coloured adhesive films (window tint) or back-painted glass. Laminated glass is saferâit holds together when broken. Use it for table tops, shower screens, and decorative walls. Test your oven's temperature accuracy first; too hot and the glass may crack. Start with small samples to perfect your timing.

lessons.title: Bending and Slumping
lessons.body: Bending and slumping shape glass using heat in a kiln. You need a kiln that reaches at least 700Â°C, plus moulds made from stainless steel, ceramic, or fibreboard. For slumping, you place glass over a mould and heat it until it softens and sags into the shape. For bending, you heat glass until it curves, often between two supports. The process: clean your glass, apply a kiln wash (like alumina hydrate) to the mould so the glass doesn't stick, then place the glass on the mould. Heat slowlyâabout 100Â°C per hourâto 600Â°C, then faster to 700â750Â°C. Watch through the peephole: the glass will start to bend. When it reaches the desired shape, hold for 10â30 minutes, then cool slowly to anneal. Annealing is critical: cool to 500Â°C, hold for 1 hour per 6 mm of thickness, then cool at 50Â°C per hour to room temperature. If you cool too fast, the glass cracks. In Africa, small kilns are available from suppliers in South Africa or imported from China. You can make simple moulds from fire bricks or ceramic fibre board. Common items: slumped bottles for cheese boards, bent glass for curved shelving, and fused bowls. Start with 3 mm glass; thicker glass takes longer. Always wear heat-resistant gloves and safety glasses. Ventilate the kiln areaâfumes from binders or dirt can be toxic. Practice with scrap glass. Bending and slumping turn flat glass into 3D art, and there's high demand for custom pieces like sinks, lampshades, and jewellery.

lessons.title: Fusing and Kiln Forming
lessons.body: Fusing is melting two or more pieces of glass together in a kiln. Kiln forming covers fusing, slumping, and casting. You need a kiln, glass that is compatible (same COEâcoefficient of expansion), and a kiln shelf with kiln wash. Start with two layers of 3 mm glass, cut to shape. Clean them with glass cleaner. Stack them on the shelf. Heat the kiln at 200Â°C per hour to 750â800Â°C. At this temperature, the glass fuses into one piece. Hold for 10â20 minutes, then cool to 500Â°C and anneal for 1 hour per 6 mm thickness. Then cool slowly. For a tack fuse (textured surface), stop at 730Â°C. For a full fuse (flat, smooth), go to 800Â°C. You can add frit (crushed glass), stringers, or copper foil for designs. In Africa, fusing is growing in studios in Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa. You can buy compatible glass from suppliers like Bullseye or Spectrum, but it's expensive. Some artisans use recycled bottle glass, but it often cracks because COE varies. Test small pieces first. Always keep a log of your firing schedules. A digital controller makes it easier. After fusing, you can slump the piece into a mould for a bowl. Or cast glass by filling a mould with glass and heating to 850Â°C. Safety: never open the kiln above 200Â°C; thermal shock can crack glass and burn you. Wear a respirator when handling frit. Fused glass sells well as jewellery, coasters, and wall art. With practice, you can create complex, multi-layered pieces. Start simple, and always anneal properly.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Decorating & Finishing Glass in an African Workshop

This module closes the loop between design intent and sellable product. In African glass value chains â from the ceramics and glass cluster in Nsam, Cameroon to architectural glazing shops in Lagos, Nairobi, Accra and Johannesburg â the margin is rarely in the raw sheet. It is in the finish: a printed logo, a fired enamel, a laminated colour, a slumped bowl. This Practical Reference is written for the workshop owner and the technician who must quote a job, buy consumables in hard currency, and deliver a repeatable result. Treat every technique here as a business process: inputs, equipment, labour hours, reject rate, and the price you can defend to a client.

1. Screen Printing on Glass

The workhorse of African architectural and beverage glass branding. A polyester or photopolymer stencil is stretched on an aluminium frame; ceramic frit ink is pushed through with a 60â90 durometer squeegee, then fired at 580â620 Â°C to fuse the enamel into the surface. For a shop in Nairobi supplying branded bottles or shower panels, one 4-colour carousel press can run 300â600 impressions per shift. Key cost drivers: mesh count (higher mesh = finer detail, thinner deposit), frit price (imported, often USD), and kiln throughput.

Table 1. Screen printing consumables and typical parameters
ParameterTypical valueBusiness note
Mesh count120â305 threads/cmFiner mesh for logos, coarser for flood coats
Emulsion thickness10â25 ÂµmThicker = denser colour, slower dry
Firing temperature580â620 Â°CMust match frit datasheet, not guesswork
Firing cycle20â40 min soakElectric kiln preferred for repeatability
Reject rate (trained shop)3â8 %Budget this into quotation

Source: parameters compiled from Ferro Corporation glass enamel technical datasheets and the Screen Printing technical library (public resources).

2. Digital Printing and Decals

UV-curable and ceramic digital printers now allow short runs â one-off corporate gifts, hotel glassware, sample panels â without the setup cost of a screen. Decals (waterslide or heat-transfer) remain the cheapest route for irregular shapes and small batches: print on decal paper, soak, slide onto the glass, fire. In West Africa, decal firing services are increasingly offered as a shared kiln service, which lets a small studio sell decorated glass without owning a kiln.

3. Painting and Staining

Cold-paint (acrylic, epoxy) gives fast turnaround for indoor decorative work; fired stains and lustres give permanence. Stains are metallic salts that bond to the glass surface at 540â600 Â°C. Lustres (gold, platinum, mother-of-pearl) are thin-film metal resinates fired at 480â560 Â°C â high-value, high-margin, but sensitive to kiln atmosphere.

Table 2. Finish durability and market positioning
TechniqueDurabilityTypical African marketRelative cost
Screen-printed enamelExcellent (fired)Bottles, architectural panels, signageMedium
Digital UV printGood (indoor)Corporate gifts, samples, short runsMediumâHigh
Decals (fired)ExcellentTableware, irregular shapesLowâMedium
Cold paintFair (indoor only)Interior dÃ©cor, craft retailLow
Stains / lustresExcellentLuxury tableware, exportHigh
Lamination (coloured PVB)Excellent (safety)Facades, balustrades, transportHigh
Slumping / fusingExcellentBowls, trophies, art piecesMediumâHigh

Source: durability ratings adapted from National Glass Association (NGA) guidance and the Bullseye Glass firing reference library (public).

4. Lamination and Coloring

Laminated glass sandwiches a coloured or printed interlayer (PVB, EVA, or SentryGlas) between two panes under heat and pressure. In Africa this is the highest-value finishing route for facades, balustrades and transport glazing because it adds safety, UV control and colour in one operation. Capital cost is real: autoclave or vacuum-bag systems, clean room conditions, and interlayer stock held in hard currency. Partner with an established laminator for your first contracts rather than buying equipment before you have orders.

5. Bending and Slumping

Slumping drapes a glass sheet over a mould at 600â700 Â°C; bending creates controlled curves for furniture and architectural panels. Mould material matters: kiln-washed ceramic fibre, stainless steel, or refractory board. Cycle time is long (6â12 hours including controlled cooling), so kiln utilisation is the economic constraint â schedule full kiln loads, never one piece at a time.

6. Fusing and Kiln Forming

Fusing bonds two or more glass layers at 750â850 Â°C. It is the technique behind coasters, jewellery, bowls and art panels sold in craft markets and hotel gift shops across the continent. The barrier to entry is a reliable electric kiln and a stable power supply; the barrier to profit is consistency. Keep a firing log for every load: date, programme, glass COE, result, rejects.

â  SAFETY WARNING â KILN AND CHEMICAL HAZARDS

  • Never open a kiln above 200 Â°C without heat-resistant gloves, apron and face shield. Thermal shock and infrared burns are the most common workshop injury.
  • Fired glass enamels and stains contain lead, cadmium or cobalt compounds. Wear a P2/N95 respirator when mixing or spraying; never eat or smoke in the finishing area.
  • Ensure kiln ventilation â fumes from lustres and decals are toxic. In shared buildings, exhaust to outside air, not into the workspace.
  • Check electrical earthing and circuit capacity. Kilns draw high current; in areas with unstable supply, use a voltage stabiliser and a dedicated breaker.
  • Keep a fire extinguisher (COâ or dry powder) and a first-aid burn kit within reach of every kiln.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm the client's end use (indoor/outdoor, safety-critical, food-contact) before choosing a technique.
  2. Verify glass COE and frit compatibility against the manufacturer datasheet â never mix brands blindly.
  3. Run a test tile for every new colour, decal or interlayer before committing the production batch.
  4. Log every kiln firing: programme, peak temperature, soak, result, rejects.
  5. Cost the job with consumables + labour + kiln time + reject allowance, not just materials.
  6. Hold imported consumables (frit, PVB, decal paper) in minimum viable stock to protect cash flow against FX swings.
  7. Train one technician as quality gate â every piece passes their inspection before packing.
  8. Photograph finished work for your portfolio; in African B2B markets, proof of past work closes the next order.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • Bullseye Glass Co. â Free Technotes & Firing Schedules
  • National Glass Association (NGA) â Industry Resources
  • Glass on Web â Technical Articles & Processing Guides
  • Ferro Corporation â Glass Enamel Product Information
  • UNIDO â Industrial Skills & SME Development Publications

Business takeaway: in African glass finishing, the technique you choose is a pricing decision. Screen printing and decals win on volume and brand work; lamination wins on architectural contracts; fusing and slumping win on margin per piece in craft and hospitality markets. Master one technique to profitability before adding the next, and let your firing log â not your memory â be the basis of every quotation.

quiz.q: What is the recommended mesh count for screen printing on glass?
quiz.explanation: 110â160 threads per inch provides good ink deposit and detail for glass printing.

quiz.q: What is the correct squeegee angle for screen printing on glass?
quiz.explanation: A 60â70Â° angle gives proper shear and ink transfer on glass.

quiz.q: How long should you expose a photo emulsion screen to sunlight for a typical design?
quiz.explanation: 2â5 minutes of sunlight exposure properly hardens the emulsion for a stencil.

quiz.q: What is a common problem in screen printing that causes paint to bleed under the stencil?
quiz.explanation: Low screen tension allows the screen to lift and paint to seep under edges.

quiz.q: Which type of glass paint requires UV curing?
quiz.explanation: UV-curable paint hardens only when exposed to UV light.

quiz.q: What is the first step before applying a water-slide decal to glass?
options: B) Clean the glass with alcohol
D) Soak the decal in water
quiz.explanation: Cleaning with alcohol removes oils and ensures the decal adheres properly.

quiz.q: How long should you soak a water-slide decal in water before applying?
quiz.explanation: 30â60 seconds allows the decal to release from its backing paper.

quiz.q: What temperature is recommended for baking a decal on glass to make it dishwasher-safe?
quiz.explanation: Baking at 150Â°C for 30 minutes sets the decal for durability.

quiz.q: Which printing method is best for short runs with complex, full-colour images?
quiz.explanation: Digital printing allows detailed, multi-colour designs without screens.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of water-slide decals over direct UV printing?
options: B) Lower cost for curved items
quiz.explanation: Decals can be applied to curved surfaces and are cheaper for small-scale work.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean glass before painting or staining?
quiz.explanation: Methylated spirits removes grease and oils that prevent paint adhesion.

quiz.q: What is 'reverse painting' on glass?
options: A) Painting the front then the back
B) Painting details first, then background on the back
quiz.explanation: In reverse painting, you paint the foreground details first on the back, then fill in the background.

quiz.q: At what temperature should you bake hand-painted glass to make it more resistant to washing?
quiz.explanation: Baking at 160Â°C for 30 minutes helps set the paint for better durability.

quiz.q: Which type of paint is easier to clean up but may need a topcoat?
quiz.explanation: Water-based paints clean up with water but are less durable without a topcoat.

quiz.q: What is a common technique for adding texture to painted glass?
quiz.explanation: A sponge creates a textured, mottled effect on glass.

quiz.q: What does EVA stand for in lamination?
quiz.explanation: EVA is ethylene vinyl acetate, a common interlayer for glass lamination.

quiz.q: What temperature range is used for EVA lamination in a vacuum bag?
quiz.explanation: EVA melts and bonds at 120â140Â°C under vacuum.

quiz.q: Why should the EVA film be cut 2â3 mm smaller than the glass?
options: B) To avoid overflow and trimming
D) To make it easier to handle
quiz.explanation: Slightly smaller film prevents excess from oozing out during lamination.

quiz.q: What is a key safety benefit of laminated glass?
options: B) It holds together when broken
quiz.explanation: Laminated glass retains its pieces when broken, reducing injury risk.

quiz.q: What is the recommended heating rate for slumping glass?
quiz.explanation: A slow rate of about 100Â°C per hour prevents thermal shock.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of kiln wash on a mould?
options: A) To make the glass shiny
B) To prevent glass from sticking
quiz.explanation: Kiln wash creates a barrier so glass doesn't fuse to the mould.

quiz.q: What is annealing in glass bending?
options: B) Slow cooling to relieve stress
quiz.explanation: Annealing is controlled slow cooling to prevent cracks and stress.

quiz.q: How long should you hold at 500Â°C during annealing for 6 mm thick glass?
quiz.explanation: Hold for 1 hour per 6 mm of thickness to anneal properly.

quiz.q: What type of glass is commonly used for slumping projects?
quiz.explanation: 3 mm glass is easier to slump and requires less time.

quiz.q: What is a common product made by slumping bottles?
quiz.explanation: Slumped bottles are often used as cheese boards or serving platters.

quiz.q: What does COE stand for in glass fusing?
quiz.explanation: COE is the coefficient of expansion, which must match for glass to fuse safely.

quiz.q: At what temperature does a full fuse typically occur?
quiz.explanation: A full fuse, where glass melts flat and smooth, occurs around 750â800Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a tack fuse?
options: B) A textured fuse at lower temperature
D) A method of cutting glass
quiz.explanation: A tack fuse is done at about 730Â°C, leaving a textured surface.

quiz.q: Why is recycled bottle glass often problematic for fusing?
quiz.explanation: Bottle glass varies in COE, causing cracks when fused with other glass.

quiz.q: What safety precaution should you take when opening a kiln?
options: A) Open it immediately after firing
quiz.explanation: Opening a kiln above 200Â°C can cause thermal shock and burns.
